claims.text: Google published the CC household expansion at 18:15 UTC on 17 September 2026.
claims.sourceLocator: Launch-page JSON-LD datePublished and published_time metadata

claims.text: Google describes CC as an early Labs experiment for adults using personal Google accounts in the United States, with existing users due an upgrade and other users directed to a waitlist.
claims.sourceLocator: s1 final availability paragraph; s4 final paragraph

claims.text: The original CC connected one person's Gmail, Calendar and Drive to prepare a daily briefing, drafts and calendar links.
The household version gives CC a separate verified Google account and allows as many as six members to collaborate with it.
claims.sourceLocator: s1 opening and How CC works section; s4 paragraphs 2-3

claims.text: Google says each member can provide selected emails, files and calendars, send material from a text message to CC by email or Google Chat, and nominate continuing email senders.
claims.sourceLocator: s1 You choose what to share and Meeting you where you are subsections

claims.text: Google says CC can produce a shared brief, calendars, tasks, documents and pre-filled forms, and can retain group or person-specific memory.
claims.sourceLocator: s1 How CC can help and Meeting you where you are subsections; s4 paragraphs 4-6

claims.text: Google says each CC instance runs on an isolated cloud computer and will not take action or share information outside the group without permission.
claims.sourceLocator: s1 verified-account and Meeting you where you are bullets

claims.text: The inspected launch page does not specify group-memory retention, source attribution for remembered facts, subgroup audiences, departure behaviour or a complete activity log.
claims.sourceLocator: Full inspected launch page; bounded claim about the page's documented contents, not the product's actual controls

claims.text: A distinct agent identity can support accountability, but it does not by itself prove source provenance, least privilege or appropriate audience selection.
claims.sourceLocator: Premises: s1 separate account and pooled outputs; s5 private-state coordination problem. Boundary: design inference, not a tested CC failure.

claims.text: Google Calendar's general guidance says personal calendar content is private unless shared and that shared-event visibility follows calendar settings with event-level controls.
claims.sourceLocator: s3 You decide what content is shared and with whom

claims.text: CalBench evaluates seven model families in a controlled private-calendar coordination benchmark with task success, disruption cost, fairness and privacy leakage as separate outcomes.

The CalBench authors report that completion alone can conceal avoidable costs and privacy or fairness trade-offs, but the benchmark does not test CC, Google services, households or real personal data.
claims.sourceLocator: s5 abstract findings and environment description; article states the non-CC boundary explicitly

claims.text: A bounded household trial should test provenance, audience, preparation versus action, correction and revocation, and membership changes with synthetic or low-sensitivity information.
claims.sourceLocator: Premises: s1 sharing, memory and action scope; s3 visibility controls; s5 separate coordination, fairness and disclosure outcomes. Recommendation is Index Us synthesis.

claims.text: Index Us did not access or test CC and cannot verify its permissions, memory, deletion controls or model behaviour.
claims.sourceLocator: Method limitation recorded by the drafter; sources were documentation and reporting rather than product access
